Left: the plane of the path at equal scales, x from −3 to 8 cm and y from −3 to 6 cm, with q = +1.0 nC at the origin (a small cross for the κ field), faint field arrows, dashed circles through A and B centred on the charge, the bold path through three draggable waypoints, and the step dℓ split into its part along the field (short black arrow, dr or dy) and its part across the field (dotted), with a thin line r from the origin to the step. Guided Inquiry

1 · The straight path

Choose the point-charge field and the straight path, keep A at 2.0 cm and B at 6.0 cm from the charge as the page opens, and press Clear. Before pressing Run, predict how the running sum of E · dℓ changes as the step moves from A to B.

2 · The arch

Keep the point-charge field, keep A and B where they are, and choose the arch path, which is about 9.8 cm long against 4.7 cm for the straight one. Before pressing Run, predict the running sum when the step reaches B.

3 · Round the far side

Keep the point-charge field and the same A and B, and choose the path round the far side of the charge, which first heads towards the charge, passes behind it and comes out to B. Before pressing Run, predict how the running sum behaves.

4 · Straight out along the field

Keep the point-charge field and the traces already in the inset, choose the straight path, and drag B along its dashed arc until it lies on the line from the charge through A, still 6.0 cm from the charge, so that the path runs straight out along the field and is only 4.0 cm long. Before pressing Run, predict the trace this run leaves in the inset.

5 · A closed loop

Keep the point-charge field and choose the closed loop, which leaves A, swings out to more than 7 cm from the charge and returns to A, with B placed on A. Before pressing Run, predict the running sum when the step is back at A.

6 · A different field

Keep the closed loop, which runs anticlockwise, and switch the field to κ(0, x, 0), which clears the inset. Before pressing Run, predict the running sum when the step is back at A.

7 · What you found

Near a point charge, only the radial part of each step counts, so ∫E·dℓ from A to B is q/4πε0 (1/rA − 1/rB), about 300 V here, whatever the path: straight, arched, round the far side or straight out.

Round any closed loop the sum is zero. That is what lets us define a potential V with ∫E·dℓ = V(A) − V(B).

The field κ(0, x, 0) fails this test: its loop sum is κ times the enclosed area, so it has curl and cannot come from charges at rest.

The Physics

The Line Integral near a Point Charge · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The line integral of a field is a sum over small steps. This sim adds up E·dℓ step by step along a path you can reshape, near a point charge, and plots the running sum against the distance from the charge.

What you'll learn

  • What a line integral adds up, one step at a time.
  • How the running sum is read against distance from the charge.
  • What a closed loop tells you about a field.
The sim's layout: the plane of the path on the left, the empty inset on the right.

What's on screen

  • Left, the plane: the charge q (orange), dashed circles through A and B, the path in black with three draggable waypoints, and the step dℓ (cyan) split into a part along the field and a part across it.
  • Right, the inset: the running sum ∫E·dℓ against r, with the last four runs kept as faint outlines in blue, violet, green and orange.
  • Sidebar: readouts of rA, rB, the step's distance r, the length covered and the sum.
See itLook at the opening state: the arch path from A, 2.0 cm from the charge, to B, 6.0 cm from it. Watch for: the orange charge, the two dashed circles, A and B on them, and an empty inset.

03

Only the part of a step along the field counts

The line integral from A to B is found by cutting the path into short steps dℓ, forming E·dℓ on each and adding the results. The charge q = +1.0 nC sits at the origin, so the field points straight away from it.

Each step splits into a part along the line from the charge, whose length is the change dr in the distance from the charge, and a part perpendicular to it. The field is radial, so only dr contributes, as in Figure 12 of the notes:

The notes' step on a point charge.

In the sim the cyan arrow is the step dℓ, the black arrow its part along the field, labelled dr, and the dotted piece the part across. Because of the 1/r² a given dr counts for more close to the charge.

Key idea. Only the change in distance from the charge enters the sum; the sideways part of a step adds nothing.
One step dℓ from a point at distance r. The black arrow is dr; the dotted piece lies along a circle about the charge.
See itStop the arch run 7.7 cm along the path, where it runs almost across the field. Watch for: the cyan step dℓ with a black dr much shorter than it, and a dotted piece for the part across.
04

The sum depends only on the two end distances

Adding the steps from rA to rB turns the integral into one of 1/r², which the notes give as (1.33):

The notes' (1.33).

For q = 1.0 nC, q/4πε0 = 8.99 V m. The path has dropped out: the sum knows only how far A and B are from the charge. For rA = 2.0 cm and rB = 6.0 cm it is 8.99 V m × (1/0.020 m − 1/0.060 m) = 300 V.

The straight path is 4.71 cm long and the arch 9.81 cm, between the same two circles, and both sums at B read 300 V. The extra length of the arch either lies across the field, which adds nothing, or goes out and comes back, which cancels.

rA
rB

These sliders move the sim's own rA and rB too. For the closed loop rB is tied to rA.

Key idea. The sum from A to B is set by rA and rB alone, whatever the path.
See itFinish the straight path from A to B, 2.0 cm and 6.0 cm from the charge. Watch for: the running sum at 300 V and the length covered at 4.71 cm.
See itFinish the arch from A to B, the same two distances. Watch for: the length covered at 9.81 cm, twice as long, and the sum at the same 300 V.
05

Every path draws the same curve against distance

The sum from A up to a point at distance r is S(r) = (q/4πε0)(1/rA − 1/r), by the same integral. It depends on r alone, so whatever the path, its trace in the inset lies on this one curve. The path decides only how far along the curve the step goes, and in which direction.

A step that moves away from the charge, with dr > 0, raises the sum, and one that moves towards it lowers the sum. The arch runs out to 6.78 cm, where S = 317 V, and returns to 6.0 cm, giving 17 V back. The far-side path first heads in to 1.59 cm, where S = −117 V, then turns out to B.

Key idea. The running sum is a height on one curve, S(r); the path never makes it longer or shorter.
S(r) for rA = 2.0 cm. The marks show the farthest points the arch and the far-side path reach.
See itFinish the straight path, then the arch, between the same A and B. Watch for: the second trace running out to 6.8 cm, 317 V, and back along the first curve to 300 V.
See itFinish the straight path, the arch and then the path round the far side. Watch for: the third trace dipping below zero near 1.6 cm and then climbing along the same curve to 300 V.
06

A closed loop returns to zero, and that makes a potential

A loop starts and ends at the same distance, so rB = rA and (1.33) gives zero however long the loop is. The sim's loop swings out to 7.38 cm and comes back: the sum climbs above 320 V on the way out and returns along the same curve to 0 V.

This is why no net work is done on a charge carried round a closed path. Since the sum depends only on the end points, the notes define the potential from a reference point (1.34):

The notes' (1.34).

For a point charge, taken from infinity, V = q/4πε0r (1.35). The sum from A to B is then V(A) − V(B), a difference of two numbers that belong to the points, not to the road between them: 449 V at 2.0 cm less 150 V at 6.0 cm.

Key idea. A zero sum round every closed loop is what lets each point carry its own potential.
The loop of the sim, anticlockwise. Where it leaves the charge, dr > 0; where it comes back, dr < 0.
See itFinish the closed loop for the point charge. Watch for: the sum climbing to a peak near 7.4 cm and falling back along the same curve to 0 V.
07

The field κ(0, x, 0) fails the loop test

Switch to κ(0, x, 0), with κ = 8.0 V/cm². It points up for x > 0, down for x < 0, and grows with x, so only the vertical part of a step counts; the sim labels it dy.

The same anticlockwise loop climbs where the field is strong and descends where it is weak, so the climb outweighs the descent. The sum round a loop is the circulation, which Stokes' theorem makes the curl times the area. Here (∇×E)z = ∂Ey/∂x − ∂Ex/∂y = κ, and the loop encloses 23.5 cm², so the sum is 8.0 V/cm² × 23.5 cm² = 188 V.

Stokes' theorem for the loop.

An electrostatic field has E = −∇V, so ∂Ex/∂y = ∂Ey/∂x. For this field the two sides are 0 and κ. No charges at rest can produce it, and it has no potential.

Key idea. A field whose loop sum is not zero has a curl and no potential.
κ(0, x, 0) as arrows, with the loop of Figure 6 and the area it encloses.
See itSwitch to κ(0, x, 0) and finish the closed loop. Watch for: the inset trace ending at 188 V, not at zero, with the step labelled dy.
08

Where it matters

  • Voltage. The voltage between two points in an electrostatic field is this line integral. It does not depend on the route, so a voltmeter reads the same with its leads laid either way round.
  • Loop sums. Round any closed path the potential differences add to zero. A field with curl, such as the electric field induced by a changing magnetic flux, breaks this, and the loop sum becomes the emf (Faraday's law, in the notes).
  • Many charges. A field of charges at rest is a sum of point-charge fields. Each has a path-independent integral, so the sum does too.
09

Summary

In one line. This sim shows how the line integral of an electric field is built up step by step along a path near a point charge.
  • Only the part of a step along the field counts, so E·dℓ = q dr/4πε0r², and the sum from A to B is (q/4πε0)(1/rA − 1/rB), about 300 V here, along any path.
  • Against r every path retraces one curve, S(r).
  • A closed loop sums to zero for a point charge, which gives a potential. κ(0, x, 0) gives 188 V and has none.

Common mix-ups

  • "A longer path collects more." The arch is twice as long as the straight path and ends at the same 300 V.
  • "Going round the charge cancels the sum." Only a path that returns to its starting distance does. The far side ends at 300 V.
  • "Every closed loop sums to zero." That is the electrostatic test, and κ(0, x, 0) fails it at +188 V.

Things to try on your own

  • Set rA and rB and check the finished sum against (1.33).
  • Drag the far-side waypoints and see how low the sum goes before it rises to B.
